Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, distinguished members of the Executive Board, We are pleased to present this proposal in response to Executive Board decision 2026/16, 2026/17, 2026/18. It seeks to establish a clear, structured and practical framework for consultation between UNICEF and the Executive Board concerning the appointment, renewal, non-renewal or termination of the heads of UNICEF independent oversight functions. The proposal covers three functions, the Director of the Office of Internal Audit and Investigations, the Director of Evaluation, and the Director of the Ethics Office. The approach is built around five principles. First, transparency and accountability. The Executive Board should receive timely and meaningful information on relevant decisions. Second, respect for the Executive Director's authority. Appointment and employment decisions remain exclusively within the authority delegated by the Secretary General to the Executive Director. which must be exercised in accordance with the applicable UN and UNICEF regulatory and policy frameworks. Third, preservation of oversight independence. Consultations must never compromise the operational independence of these functions or the ability to discharge the mandate objectively and impartially.

Fourth.

Due process and confidentiality. Personnel matters and sensitive information will only be shared to the extent legally permissible while protecting individual rights and the integrity of any ongoing proceedings. And fifth, continuity of oversight. Whenever a term is renewed, not renewed or ended early, Consultation will help ensure a smooth transition and uninterrupted effective oversight. More concretely, for appointment, UNICEF would notify the Executive Board before recruitment begins and share the approved qualifications and terms of appointment. Following appointment, UNICEF would provide the Executive Board with the appointee's professional profile and agreed term. For renewal and non-renewal, UNICEF would inform the Executive Board as appropriate and share the applicable regulatory framework, transition arrangements, and recruitment timetable while respecting confidentiality and due process. In cases of termination, the same principle would apply with additional information on continuity measures and where relevant, interim arrangements. In terms of the modalities of consultation, those could take place through confidential informal briefings, close meeting with the Bureau, or written observation depending on the circumstances and sensitivity of the matter. The modality would be subject to periodic review by the Executive Director taking account of experience, good governance practices, and Executive Board feedback. while safeguarding the independence of the oversight functions. UNICEF hopes that this proposal strikes the right balance, transparency and consultation for the Executive Board while preserving the Executive Director's authority, due process, confidentiality and the independence of UNICEF's oversight functions. Thank you.

The fourth track, the data quint, is advancing a shared humanitarian model, data model that improves interoperability and evidence-based decision making, all of it underpinned by robust data protection, privacy safeguards and governance. The bottom line of success for this work package is whether the UN system that emerges is better able to deliver for children, particularly in very fragile situations, deliver faster, more efficiently and with greater collective impact. Next, please. Work package five on country configurations. Four points here. This working group has identified 17 countries as part of the first mover cohort to pilot a revived approach to aligning country configuration with cooperation framework implementation. Second, UNICEF very much welcomes a more needs-based, differentiated, context-specific UN presence that is guided by national priorities, agency mandates, and comparative advantage, while recognizing no one-size-fits-all. And UNICEF is applying these very principles internally in the implementation of our new strategic plan. under the lead of DED programs. For example, 16 country offices are now being consolidated into five multi-country office configurations. The third point here is in this work package, executive board governance must be preserved. with country program documents remaining the formal accountability framework for linking cooperation framework priorities to UNICEF's programmatic commitments, allocation of resources and results for children. Fourth, this work package is complemented in parallel by the work package on regional reset, which applies the same test. Any regional technical expertise or non-resident capacity must strengthen country level delivery and not add parallel coordination layers. In short, the bottom line for success distinguished delegates, is whether the right capabilities are present in the right places for children who depend on them. A simplified structural configuration should look good not only on paper, but must deliver, as was said, for children in remote communities, conflict zones, and middle-income countries seeped in high inequalities. Next, please. Work package 14 on unified services roadmap, three points. First, business operations strategies have helped us generate more than $100 million in cumulative savings since 2019. Second, 53% of UNICEF's offices are currently on common premises as against the system-wide average of 32%. So for example, we provide payroll, HR administration and learning services to sister agencies, and in the same vein, we also benefit from system wide services such as UN booking hub and fleet from WFP and UNHCR in over 200 locations. The bottom line is When administrative processes are streamlined, more resources, both human and financial, can be freed up and redirected to children. And this has real tangible consequences. It means faster movement of life-saving supplies and more time available to frontline workers to engage with communities. At the end of the day, efficiency is not just about cutting costs, it's about saving lives. Next, please. Work package 16 on UN system data commons, UNICEF continues to co-lead this work package under the leadership of our executive director together with UNDESA and EOSG. And two quick points. First, this work package is turning UN data reform into visible implementation and we are thrilled that 28 UN entities have now committed to sharing official public data through the Data Commons platform and delighted to share that this platform will be launched later this month, allowing users to query, browse, visualize and download harmonized UN data for the first time. Second, while this work rests on strong technical foundation, as has been highlighted on the slide, its value is not only technical, because better AI readiness, interoperability, and easier access to trusted data means that governments and partners can act more quickly. And that is the bottom line for success because governments can't plan for children that they can't see and better data means children are seen, they are counted and they are included in decisions that affect their lives. Next please. That's the last work package which is work package 18 on funding mechanisms and two quick points. First is only 6% of UNICEF's total public sector income in 2025 was core, as you heard in the opening session. It was one of the lowest on record in UNICEF's history. Under the funding compact that member states signed up to in 2024, member states committed to 30% of their contributions being core. If we match the contributions of Member States from last year, this figure against the funding compact benchmark comes to only 11%. This means that for every dollar a government gave UNICEF last year, 89 cents arrived as earmarked. Second, taken together, these figures point to a wider concern. This is not just a question of volume of funding, but it's also about quality of funding, because more tightly earmarked, shorter term funding increases transaction costs and limits our ability to adapt, plan and deliver at scale for children. The bottom line of success is a funding mix where core thematic pulled and earmarked each playing its part as committed by member states in the funding compact. Any narrowing of this funding mix risks interrupting services for children and those most affected are those furthest behind from the support. Next, please. In conclusion, two points. First, Distinguished delegates, as you can see, encouraging progress is emerging. We look forward to the SG's report later this month as an opportunity to assess progress across the system, while we remain clear eyed on three priorities. delivering for children on the ground in the most vulnerable contexts where needs are the greatest while safeguarding our normative responsibility for child rights. B, ensuring that reform implementation is paced and sequenced responsibly because reform must not move faster than field systems can safely absorb. And we can't afford disrupting service delivery in pursuit of change. C, improving the quality of funding while remaining transparent with this board on the cost implications of reform. Next, please. The second point is, sorry, just to conclude the slide, the executive board can count on UNICEF to report progress transparently and we will continue to seek your guidance as decisions are taken and implementation unfolds. A last word, distinguished delegates, the choices we make now will determine whether this moment of reform translates from ambition into tangible impact, and children must remain the central yardstick of whether this reform succeeds. I thank you, Mr. President, and over to you.

Mr. President, Madam Executive Director, distinguished members of the Executive Board, I have the honour to deliver the statement on behalf of a group of countries, Australia, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Japan, the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Norway, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, the United Kingdom, the European Union as a donor, and my own country, Germany. We appreciate the concrete examples and figures, for instance, on integrated supply chains. common services and the data commons. Against this background, we would like to raise three questions for further clarification. First, on the pace and sequencing of reforms. We appreciate UNICEF's emphasis on ensuring that UNAD reforms are evidence-based and carefully sequenced. so that implementation does not outpace the capacity of field operations to manage change. Here we would welcome UNICEF's assessment of the effects of multiple concurrent reform processes. Where does UNICEF see the greatest risks to operations in humanitarian and fragile contexts and what measures are being taken to manage those risks? Second, on country presence and program delivery, Regarding the implications of country configuration decisions for UNICEF, could you please elaborate on the specific criteria and thresholds that agencies should apply when assessing whether their presence can be reduced, consolidated or replaced by another model? Also, keeping in mind that UN country team configuration is not only about whether to maintain presence, but also about rethinking what kind of presence is required and financially sustainable. How are you approaching and calibrating this aspect? Third point on resources and opportunity costs. UNICEF acknowledges that engagement across multiple UNAD work packages creates additional demands and opportunity costs for program delivery. Could you please provide further detail on the resource implications of UNICEF's participation in UNAT, including effects on staff workload, organizational capacity and program delivery? On a more general role, our perspective on UNAT is guided by several key elements. It is essential that the UN delivers as one and moves decisively to implement reforms of the UN development system agreed several years ago. At country level, delivery must be at the core of reform efforts. We see a need to empower the resident and humanitarian coordinators to strengthen coordination, coherence and transparency within UN country teams. National ownership should remain central with UN entities work clearly derived from the sustainable development cooperation frameworks and assessed against concrete results and national development priorities. At the regional level, we believe that roles, mandates and responsibilities need to be clearly defined with regional capacities designed to support country level implementation.

We do take this very seriously, as you will have seen from the many engagements that we've had with many of you. And to the question that Germany asked, not that I can give you a precise mathematical figure, but of course it comes at a cost. Everybody on this podium is intensely engaged at the highest level to make sure that we steer this to something that is tangible, meaningful in terms of the results for people that need us. Our many colleagues in the regional offices, in the country offices, our programmatic colleagues, all of us are working to make sure that the UN as a whole can deliver more, better and different in a time where we have just downsized the organization, where the funding needs are growing. and staff has been cut. So does it hurt sometimes? I will be very honest, yes. But we cannot not afford to engage because as the UN system as a whole, as UNICEF turns 80 and the UN is 80, we have to stop, reflect and see how we can do better for humanity. There were a couple of questions asked that pointed to risks of UN reform settings and particularly risks in, you know, the situations where there is a difference between life and death in fragile settings and humanitarian settings. And I just wanted to point out we are very much aware of these risks. In the information note we submitted to the board, look at section D where we outline in writing also where we as UNICEF perceive certain risks For example, the risk that child specific mandates, expertise and accountability becomes less distinct in a reconfigured setting in a broader framework. That configuration may lead to produce presence and for children, a reduced presence isn't a design feature on paper. It has a real consequence in terms of is there an agency that is able to deliver Immediate health services when they are needed, child protection services when they are needed. Presence has a meaning beyond an office. So for us, that is what we see as one of the major risks. And as we are very much result focused, that is one thing that we will keep front and center. I think the second risk really relates to, and it was remarked this morning by our executive director, Ms. O'Brien referenced it, the quality of the funding and where we are going, and that has a major impact on our ability to be there reliably with the agility required with timely support. And for that, we need a balanced funding architecture. And if I just take the example of Ebola, when the Ebola crisis started, within 24 hours, we were able to deploy resources from core to ensure that we could do first outreach for the pandemic that was needed. The second immediate complementary tranche was from the Global Thematic Fund for Humanitarian Action because it's flexible funding we can deploy as and when the need arises. That was then complemented by logistics support, by support from our supply division, by bilateral earmarked resources, and ultimately also by funding, by pooled funding. But pooled funding in the way it comes to agencies, whether it's us or any other UN agency, very often is not flexible, is not agile, because it comes to us as projectized. So there are different forms of fundings that we need as UN to be as reliable, as flexible, and as predictable for children that need us. I think there is an issue that was raised also in terms of how fast can you do reform. without losing quality of services on which children's lives and livelihoods depend. We see that there is a risk of disruption if we move too fast, and we are looking at Reducing programmatic continuity, delivery of services in the field, is there a risk? We need to keep that top of mind. Is there a risk of weakened specialized expertise, not just ours, but also of certain normative agencies? Is there a risk that our operational capacity to deliver would be diminished, especially again in fragile and high need context? Are there additional burdens, transaction burdens, by the way we are reconfiguring how we operate together and how do we deal with that. Most of these issues come to the fore most pressingly in humanitarian settings where literally lives are at risk if we are not timely enough. We strongly believe that we have to engage, we will continue to engage and the way we try to look at this is that for all of these risks we look at mitigation measures and these mitigation measures we keep front and center. Every dialogue, every work package, every reform track, we're looking at what is the evidence-based solution-oriented results focused entry points for children. And for every work package, we have a good idea of what that looks like. In some of the recent discussions we've been asked as UNICEF considering the deep bench of expertise that we have on monitoring and evaluation and data work, can we help design an impact oriented indicator framework to measure what success looks like on UN reform, particularly for example on the country configuration. That's not a UNICEF framework, it will be an impact related framework. That's how we keep track of how well we are doing and how we mitigate those risks. In the end, and I think if I recall well, Ms. O'Brien mentioned it during the last meeting in June that we had the annual session, the metric of success of UN reform is not, again, whether it looks good on paper. But a mother when she comes with her sick child with cholera in a clinic is not going to look at is it work package 18 or work package 4 or 3. Which reform track has this been discussed? She will look at do I get the medication in time? Is there a trained nurse to tend to my child? And is there a system in place that can prevent this from happening? Again, and again, that has to be at the end of the day, the lens through which every discussion, every decision we take needs to be looked at. We're talking about a third of humanity that is children, and it's 50% of those that are in the bracket of extreme poor. And we simply have to do better, all of us together as member states, as UNICEF, and the UN as a whole. And with that, I turn it to Ms. O'Brien.

Thank you, Didi Kiti. So just to compliment and a few points from my side, but let me start by first thanking the distinguished delegate from Guatemala and some of the other delegates who have emphasized the importance of national priorities. And if I may just take that a step further in terms of investing in national systems and local systems as was emphasized by our executive director. Because even in acute crisis situations, as UNICEF, our job is not to set up parallel systems. It is to make sure that we invest in systems no matter how fragile they are so that we can prevent them from further collapse. And we have several examples of doing so. So thank you for raising that point. I want to thank the distinguished delegate of Germany and all the other members of the executive board who joined up in the strong support, but also in terms of highlighting several important points. So let me compliment on the question of risks. And in a way, if you look at risks, it's also about costs of reform. And then if you invert the risks and costs, it's also there are opportunities which we've talked about. So just very briefly, two things on this. First is UNICEF in many ways is unique in the UN system. I for one have worked with other UN agencies and I'd say the The main uniqueness is that we have a dual mandate. We operate in both humanitarian and development contexts. And of course, we have a child rights mandate too. But one of the risks that we see is less funding being available in the development settings. And of course, we know we are doing the hyper prioritization in the humanitarian and fragile contexts. And I'll come to that in a moment. But in the development context itself, it's critically important for us to invest in preparedness, in anticipatory action, in prevention, as well as in recovery efforts. for crisis situations. And maybe just a good example of this, if I may just turn to Germany, the assistance that you give us through your transitional development assistance budget, which is resilience focused in the Sahel region across five countries, which last year enabled us together with WFP to reach 6 million vulnerable people, 50% of them being children. And these investments are happening in that nexus. It's both development and humanitarian. And I think that in a way is one of our big worries is the funding going to be impacting these situations when the demand to invest in these situations is really, is very real. The second point on this is about transaction costs. And in a way, I think the US also mentioned about the distinguished delegate from the US about concrete actions and how can member states help. And this is where I think Kitty already spoke to some of the costs that we are facing as we navigate a lot of processes and a lot of demands for reporting. as we are cutting down our own capacity, painful cuts, but yet trying to stay the course for children to make sure that we remain relentless in delivering for children more and better. And concretely, I wanted to give some facts here. Last year in 2025, we saw a 113% increase in donor reporting as compared to 2018, and a part of this is explained with increasing trend of earmarked funding. This is again very real. We do value the earmarked funding, but we also recognize it comes with much more burden of reporting. Similarly, we saw in this period a 73% increase in donor financial statements. So again, all this to say, while these are very important aspects which we continue to monitor, and report on, it also means that the more transaction costs we have to shoulder, the more time it takes away from programming and delivering for children. In fact, sometimes if we were to be very direct, we feel that some of our technical experts are also turning into grant managers, and which of course they have to be, but just making sure that we have a bit of a balance. The rise in earmarked funding, which is also a risk, is coming with heavily projectized oversight mechanisms. And we do see increasing donor conditionalities and each conditionality requires tailored monitoring, oversight and reporting. So this is again an area where we look forward to working with you and in hand in hand to find pragmatic solutions that can enable us to be as efficient as possible and as effective in reaching the most vulnerable as you have asked us to. Let me just touch on the question around the thresholds and criteria which Kitty spoke to a bit, but maybe just to complement two points. The first is we as UNICEF very much support, as I mentioned in the presentation, a differentiated evidence-based approach to the country configuration and the presence. We do recognize that in many situations, we are many of us. And I think that what we think that what is important, and we are having these discussions in the UN system-wide working group on country configurations, is that configuration changes that reduce presence, particularly in fragile and high need contexts, they do have direct consequences for children, as was said. It means whether children survive or die or whether vaccines reach them before an outbreak does. So we've got to be pragmatic and sensible, and we believe that the core test is whether the configuration makes the UN development system more effective for children, not less present where the needs are the greatest. In the second point here, in terms of concrete parameters, which is very much guided by our own operational experience on the ground, including in the context of the new strategic plan implementation, we have shared these parameters with the rest of the system. For example, A is the threshold is about protecting program delivery in fragile and high need context. B is preserving capacity for normative mandates. And in that regard is our own commitment to child rights. C is reflecting the differentiated country context based on an interplay of income and fragility D is drawing and harnessing, uh, the fullest strength of the different agencies, including specialized agencies, our respective comparative advantages, rather than exclusively focusing on physical headcount. And last but not the least, the parameter threshold, call it whatever, is the full consultation and engagement with host governments, which of course is critical for us. I think it's too early for us to report on progress in some of these work packages. You also mentioned the regional reset in your joint statement, just to acknowledge that there is some good work happening there. And again, we supportive. We feel that the regional reset can bring an opportunity to improve and increase cross-pillar coherence, as well as increase our expertise on foresight, political economy analysis, bringing most specialized expertise to tackle sub-regional challenges and cross-border operations. But at the same time, It is important for us to be very clear eyed that this regional reset and the regional layer must ultimately solve country level problems and not add another layer to it. And it should be able to leverage the operational expertise on the ground of our regional offices and that of our sister agencies and the regional economic commissions. Again, this is work in progress and we very much look forward It's still early days. We very much look forward to some of these pilots moving along the way. And that, in a way, also addresses the question on next steps. So I thank you, Mr. President, and turn it back to you.

I thank the Secretariat for their remarks. If there are no additional comments, we shall consider the update on the UNAT initiative and implementation by UNICEF later in the session under agenda item 13, the adoption of draft decisions. Distinguished delegates, before we adjourn for the day, I believe that the Secretary of the Executive Board, Mr. Andres Franco, would like to make an announcement. Mr. Secretary, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President. Distinguished delegates, in consultation with Grete, I would like to tell you that the informal consultations will be held in this conference room, 30. So instead of five that we had initially said, we're just trying to use the time since everybody's here, 30. 30 is good, no? Good, thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the Secretary for this announcement. This brings us to the end of day one. Thank you very much for good work.
